title: Fill the input sheets
guide-section: Working with a case
bread-crumbs: false
---

An economist does not type seventy fields by hand. You start from the shipped template snapshot and replace the cells you would have edited in yellow on Input 1–8.

```{python}
import pandas as pd

from lic_dsf_2025_08_12 import api, data

inputs = api.ExternalDsaRiskRatingSignalInputs.from_defaults()
len(inputs.__dataclass_fields__)
```

`compute_external_dsa_risk_rating_signal` needs 74 leaves; the overall rating needs 86. Each name is the snake_case form of an Input-sheet series. The matching default lives on `data` as `{NAME}_DEFAULT`. Unknown override names fail closed.

`from_workbook(path)` binds the same leaves from a populated workbook of this vintage, then accepts the same overrides.

## Discover fields with `describe()`

You do not need to guess field names. Every `*Inputs` bundle has a `describe()` class method. It returns a dictionary from field name to an `InputField` with four things on it: whether the field is a scalar or a series (and over which axes), the allowed values, the template default, and the worksheet cell behind each value. Call it before you write any overrides:

```{python}
fields = api.ExternalDsaRiskRatingSignalInputs.describe()

pd.DataFrame(
    [
        [
            name,
            ", ".join(axis.name for axis in field.axes) or "scalar",
            field.size,
            next(iter(field.cells.values())),
        ]
        for name, field in fields.items()
    ],
    columns=["Field", "Axes", "Values", "First cell"],
).head(12).style.hide(axis="index")
```

Drop `.head(12)` to see all 74 fields. For a single field, read the attributes directly:

```{python}
tailored = fields["input6_tailored_tests_enabled"]
print("allowed values:", tailored.values)
print("default:", tailored.default)
print("cell:", tailored.cells[()])
```

`values` is the type annotation of one value. A `Literal[...]` lists the only choices the model accepts. A plain `str` (for example `country`) is checked against the template's own lists when the bundle is built, not by the annotation. Scalar fields have one cell, keyed by the empty coordinate `()`.

For a series, `axes` gives the axis names and their keys, and `cells` maps each coordinate to its worksheet cell. This is how you find the cell to edit in Excel for one creditor or one year:

```{python}
rates = fields["input4_interest_rate"]
gdp = fields["input3_input_3_macro_gross_domestic_product_us_dollars"]
pd.DataFrame(
    [
        ["input4_interest_rate", "INSTRUMENT", rates.axes[0].keys[:4], rates.cells[("IMF",)]],
        [
            "input3_input_3_macro_gross_domestic_product_us_dollars",
            "TIME_PERIOD",
            gdp.axes[0].keys[:4],
            gdp.cells[(2024,)],
        ],
    ],
    columns=["Field", "Axis", "First keys", "Cell for IMF / 2024"],
).style.hide(axis="index")
```

Each bundle describes only the fields its function reads. To find out whether an assumption affects a given output, check whether its name is in that bundle's `describe()`.

## Scalars you change first

These are the Input 1 / Input 2 / Input 6 switches that usually move first in a new vintage:

```{python}
pd.DataFrame(
    [
        ["country", data.COUNTRY_DEFAULT],
        ["first_projection_year", data.FIRST_PROJECTION_YEAR_DEFAULT],
        ["discount_rate", data.DISCOUNT_RATE_DEFAULT],
        ["external_domestic_debt_definition", data.EXTERNAL_DOMESTIC_DEBT_DEFINITION_DEFAULT],
        ["input_1_rer_overvaluation", data.INPUT_1_RER_OVERVALUATION_DEFAULT],
        ["input6_tailored_tests_enabled", data.INPUT6_TAILORED_TESTS_ENABLED_DEFAULT],
        ["contingent_liability_soe_debt_pct_gdp", data.CONTINGENT_LIABILITY_SOE_DEBT_PCT_GDP_DEFAULT],
        [
            "contingent_liability_financial_market_pct_gdp",
            data.CONTINGENT_LIABILITY_FINANCIAL_MARKET_PCT_GDP_DEFAULT,
        ],
        ["ppp_capital_stock_shock_pct", data.PPP_CAPITAL_STOCK_SHOCK_PCT_DEFAULT],
    ],
    columns=["Field", "Snapshot"],
).style.hide(axis="index")
```

| Workbook cell | Field | Allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Input 1 `C7` | `country` | LIC-DSF country names as spelled in the template (`Gambia, The`, `Congo, DR`, …) |
| Input 1 `C18` | `first_projection_year` | Integer year |
| Input 1 `C25` | `discount_rate` | Decimal in `[0, 1]` — `0.05` is 5 percent, not `5` |
| Input 1 `C31` | `input_1_rer_overvaluation` | Percent overvaluation |
| Input 1 `C33` | `external_domestic_debt_definition` | `Residency-based` or `Currency-based` |
| Input 6 `C6` | `input6_tailored_tests_enabled` | `On` or `Off` |

The package validates those domains before the formulas run. A misspelled country name or a discount rate of `5` (instead of `0.05`) fails closed:

```{python}
try:
    api.ExternalDsaRiskRatingSignalInputs.from_defaults(discount_rate=5)
except ValueError as error:
    str(error)
```

## Macro and financing series

Input 3–5 are labeled `Series` objects — immutable tensors with named axes, not plain lists. Nominal GDP on Input 3 is a single `TIME_PERIOD` axis covering history and the projection:

```{python}
gdp = data.INPUT3_INPUT_3_MACRO_GROSS_DOMESTIC_PRODUCT_US_DOLLARS_DEFAULT
print("axes:", [axis.name for axis in gdp.domain.axes])
print("years:", gdp.domain.axes[0].keys[0], "…", gdp.domain.axes[0].keys[-1])
print("2024 GDP:", gdp.sel(TIME_PERIOD=2024))
```

`sel` drops the axes you fix. For a one-axis series that is just the observation. You can also index with the year itself (`gdp[2024]`) or the coordinate tuple (`gdp[(2024,)]`).

Input 4 interest rates are keyed by `INSTRUMENT` — the same creditor rows as the external-financing sheet:

```{python}
rates = data.INPUT4_INTEREST_RATE_DEFAULT
pd.DataFrame(
    [
        [instrument, rates.sel(INSTRUMENT=instrument)]
        for instrument in ("IMF", "Eurobond", "PPG ST external debt")
    ],
    columns=["Instrument", "Interest rate"],
).style.hide(axis="index")
```

Exports of goods and services (Input 3) use the same year axis as GDP:

```{python}
exports = data.INPUT3_INPUT_3_MACRO_EXPORTS_OF_GOODS_AND_SERVICES_DEFAULT
exports.sel(TIME_PERIOD=2024)
```

## Override one cell, keep the rest

Pass keyword overrides into `from_defaults`. The call below is the Excel action “type 4 percent in Input 1 `C25`”:

```{python}
api.compute_external_dsa_risk_rating_signal(
    api.ExternalDsaRiskRatingSignalInputs.from_defaults(discount_rate=0.04)
)
```

To edit a time series, rebuild it with `with_records` so the schema and cell provenance stay attached. The example raises 2024 nominal GDP and leaves every other year untouched:

```{python}
gdp = data.INPUT3_INPUT_3_MACRO_GROSS_DOMESTIC_PRODUCT_US_DOLLARS_DEFAULT
gdp_revised = gdp.with_records(
    (coord, 50_000.0 if coord == (2024,) else value)
    for coord, value in gdp.items()
)
pd.DataFrame(
    [
        ["2024 template", gdp.sel(TIME_PERIOD=2024)],
        ["2024 revised", gdp_revised.sel(TIME_PERIOD=2024)],
        ["2025 unchanged", gdp_revised.sel(TIME_PERIOD=2025)],
    ],
    columns=["Year", "Nominal GDP"],
).style.hide(axis="index")
```

Pass `gdp_revised` as `input3_input_3_macro_gross_domestic_product_us_dollars` in `from_defaults`.

Two-axis series (Input 4 disbursements are `INSTRUMENT` × `TIME_PERIOD`; customized public deltas are `INDICATOR` × `TIME_PERIOD`) use the same pattern: iterate `items()`, change the coordinates you care about, and call `with_records`.

## Sheet → field groups

| Workbook sheet | Typical fields |
| --- | --- |
| Input 1 – Basics | `country`, `first_projection_year`, `discount_rate`, `external_domestic_debt_definition`, `input_1_rer_overvaluation` |
| Input 2 – Debt coverage | `contingent_liability_*_pct_gdp`, `ppp_capital_stock_shock_pct` |
| Input 3 – Macro-debt | `input3_input_3_macro_*`, `input3_input_3_external_debt_*`, `input3_domestic_*`, `input3_old_debt_service`, `input3_new_disbursements` |
| Input 4 – External financing | `input4_interest_rate`, `input4_grace_period`, `input4_loan_maturity`, `input4_disbursements`, `input4_blend_variant` |
| Input 5 – Local-debt financing | `input5_grace_period`, `input5_interest_rate_on_domestic_debt`, `input5_maturity`, `input5_gfn_share` |
| Input 6 – Tailored / standard tests | `input6_tailored_tests_enabled`, `input6_commodity_group_relevant`, `input6_standard_*` |
| Input 8 – SDR | `input8_sdr_stock`, `input8_sdr_interest_rate` |
| Customized scenario – public | `customized_public_include_scenario`, `customized_public_delta`, overflow and initial-stock scalars |

::: {.callout-tip}
Keep one `from_defaults(...)` call in your notebook. Change one keyword, re-run the rating functions, and you have a one-assumption sensitivity — the same discipline as shocking a single yellow cell and pressing F9.
:::
